title: Foreign Investors Pump $7.5 Billion Into Indian Equities in Ten Sessions
excerpt: The November inflow is the highest monthly figure in five years on Bloomberg data, reversing a year of heavy FPI selling — while domestic institutions book profits into a near-10% rally.
body:
• Foreign portfolio investors pumped $7.5 billion into Indian equities in the first 10 trading sessions of November, the highest monthly inflow in five years, according to Bloomberg data reported by the Economic Times.
  • The buying reverses months of selling: FPIs withdrew $2.17 billion in October and $3.46 billion in September, and pulled $13.23 billion in March alone.
  • Fund managers credit profit-taking in global AI stocks, a near-21% fall in Brent crude, a stronger rupee and cheaper Indian valuations after a two-year correction.
  • Domestic institutions moved the other way, selling more than Rs 49,000 crore in the same 10 sessions as the Sensex and Nifty gained nearly 10%.

Foreign portfolio investors have returned to Indian equities at a pace not seen in five years. FPIs pumped $7.5 billion into Indian shares in the first 10 trading sessions of November — the highest monthly inflow in five years, according to Bloomberg data reported by the Economic Times. Net investment so far this month is the highest since November 2021; the last month with a larger inflow was November 2020, at $9.56 billion.

Measured differently, the streak looks bigger still. CNBC-TV18 reported, citing provisional exchange data, that Friday was the tenth consecutive session of FPI buying, taking net purchases in November to $9.08 billion. The two compilations use different data and cut-off points, but they agree on the direction and the scale of the reversal — and on the benchmark: November 2020's $9.6 billion remains the largest monthly purchase on record.

What is driving the money back

Fund managers point to several forces arriving at once: a correction in AI-related stocks globally that has investors booking profits there, a sharp fall in crude oil, and Indian valuations that look cheaper after a two-year correction. "The FPI flows are driven by multiple factors — profit booking on AI investments, drop in oil prices, election results in Brazil, correction in Indian valuations over last two years, talks of exemptions on capital gains and reduction in rupee volatility," said Nilesh Shah, managing director of Kotak Mahindra AMC.

The oil and currency moves behind that view are concrete. Brent crude has fallen nearly 21%, to $93.37 a barrel on November 13, from a peak of $118 on October 30. The rupee has appreciated by Rs 1.97, about 2%, against the US dollar since the beginning of October, reaching Rs 94.25 by mid-November; CNBC-TV18 noted the rupee is the best-performing Asian currency over the past month.

Global brokerages have shifted stance alongside the flows. HSBC upgraded India to Overweight from Neutral, and Citi, Bernstein and CLSA have also turned more positive, CNBC-TV18 reported. The Nifty 50 trades at 18.3 times one-year forward earnings, below its five-year average of 19.3 times, according to Bloomberg data.

Domestic investors are selling into the rally

The counterpart to the foreign buying is domestic profit-booking. Domestic institutional investors sold equities worth more than Rs 49,000 crore in the first 10 trading sessions of November, according to NSE data — after providing the market's backstop through much of the year. Since the start of November, the Sensex and the Nifty have each gained nearly 10%, while the BSE MidCap 150 and BSE SmallCap 250 indices have advanced around 8% each.

The year this reverses

The November surge follows the heaviest sustained selling in years. FPIs began 2026 by withdrawing $3.26 billion in January, returned briefly with $1.69 billion of buying in February, then pulled out $13.23 billion in March — their biggest monthly sell-off. September saw $3.46 billion leave and October $2.17 billion. By mid-October, foreign investors had offloaded nearly $33 billion of Indian equities in 2026, CNBC-TV18 reported.

What to watch

Whether this becomes a trend rather than a burst is the open question. "Lower crude prices, better earnings and now attractive valuations seem to have supported this sentiment change. This is a positive signal but may be early to be extrapolated; the fundamentals must improve and the oil and currency stability must hold for this to become a sustained trend," said Anurag Byas, director for global markets solutions at Rothschild & Co. The immediate marker is the month-end total: with more than a week of trading left in November, the inflow is chasing November 2020's $9.6 billion record.
